summary: A memo of data transfer rates seen between Rand and UCLA when sending card decks and receiving files through UCLA's remote job service. The measured rates were in the range of roughly 8,000 to almost 20,000 bits per second. It lists reasons for slowness, including disk contention and slow operating system interrupt handling.

eli5.summary: Some people timed how fast files moved between two cities and found it slower than hoped. They list the reasons, such as busy disks and slow computers.

questions: rand ucla remote job service speed
why were early arpanet transfers slow
subtitle: Measured file transfer rates between Rand and UCLA in 1971, and the reasons they were slow.

tldr.problem: The authors wanted to show typical data rates for their use of RJS at UCLA CCN.
tldr.mechanism: A memo lists timings for sending card decks to UCLA and receiving files back, with block size and rate for each run, taken at night when little else was happening.
tldr.outcome: Rates ranged from 8000 to 19600 bits per second, and blocking made about a 2:1 difference on sending. It updates RFC 113.

today: RFC 227 updates RFC 113. It records 1971 measurements; the metadata lists its status as Unknown and no later RFC as replacing it.

sections.title: Why Transfers Were Slow
sections.content: The attached memo shows data rates typical of Rand's use of RJS at UCLA CCN. Earlier, more detailed timing tests with UCSB showed most time was lost because of four things: channel contention with their disk drive access; their NCP running at higher priority than batch jobs but lower than text editing and interactive graphics; very slow OS interrupt handling on both ends; and spooling time on the remote system.
sections.eli5: Busy disks, a busy computer and slow handling of interruptions all slowed the files down.

sections.title: The Measurements
sections.content:
The memo was taken at night when little else was happening on their 65. Sending to UCLA, 642 cards of 80 bytes took 50 seconds (8218 bits per second), 375 cards of 80 bytes took 30 seconds (8000) and 509 cards at a block size of 800 bytes took 20 seconds (16288).

Receiving from UCLA, the file had a blocksize of 1330 bytes and each line was assumed to be 100 bytes. 4900 lines took 200 seconds (19600), 872 lines took 47 seconds (14843) and 3900 lines took 185 seconds (16865).
sections.eli5: They sent and received piles of cards and lines and timed each one.

sections.title: Blocking Helps
sections.content: The memo concludes from the send figures that blocking makes about a 2:1 difference. Memory also recalls a 2 or 3 to 1 advantage for blocking on receive when unblocked files were coming from UCSB. The RFC updates RFC 113.
sections.eli5: Sending files in bigger bundles roughly doubled the speed.
